newsitem.title: UK: UK jobless rate falls to lowest level for 6 years.
newsitem.headline: UK jobless rate falls to lowest level for 6 years.

text.p: Britain's jobless rate has fallen to its lowest level for six years in a welcome boost for the embattled Conservative government as it starts an election campaign way behind in opinion polls.
Official statistics released on Wednesday showed that unemployment fell by 68,200 in February to 1.75 million, or 6.2 percent of the workforce.
It was the lowest total jobless figure since October 1990 and the 12th consecutive monthly fall.
Prime Minister John Major, facing the prospect of defeat in elections on May 1, welcomed the jobless fall.

"Today's news is proof that Britain is booming...Falling unemployment, stable prices, lower taxes, higher living standards -- people's hard work has created a turbo-economy, which is making life better right across the country," Major added.
The economic data also showed unexpected strength in retail sales, which rose 0.5 percent in February, indicating a return of consumer confidence.
But average earnings rose by an unexpected 5.0 percent in January, the highest figure since November 1992.

That rise in earnings sent worrying signals that the British economy might be steaming ahead too fast, putting pressure on interest rates -- currently at six percent -- for whichever government is elected in six weeks' time.

"The UK data are not strong enough to trigger a pre-election rate hike, but the jump in earnings will boost speculation that a post-election tightening could be as large as 50 basis points (half a percentage point)," said Bank of America economist Jeremy Hayward.

The Conservatives, racked by divisions over Europe and suffering from a "time for a change" feeling among Britons after 18 years in power, are around 25 points behind the opposition Labour Party in opinion polls.
Major has predicted that as voting day nears, the booming economy will influence Britons to come back to his party.
Labour condemned the fall in unemployment as "fantasy figures" saying that in one in five households, families have no one in work.
